title: Why CEOs Eventually Outgrow EOS
author: Trammell, J.
summary: Consultant J. Trammell argues that the popular Entrepreneurial Operating System (EOS), while excellent for owner-operators, breaks down once a company scales past roughly 50 employees or the founder becomes accountable to outside shareholders and a board. He contends EOS assumes a single decision-maker (the 'Integrator') and doesn't account for a board-accountable CEO's need to build and delegate to an executive team, citing private-equity data that 65 percent of PE firms report CEO turnover during a holding period. He introduces his own 'Chief Executive Operating System' as the framework built specifically for that harder, board-accountable job.
points: Distinguishes the owner-operator job EOS was designed for from the board-accountable CEO job, which involves outside authority and a full executive team.
Cites a 65 percent CEO-turnover rate among PE-held companies as evidence of how poorly that job transition is currently supported.
Notes that EOS Worldwide itself acknowledges the system wasn't built for companies with investors and boards.
Positions the author's own 'Chief Executive Operating System' as the missing framework for CEOs managing at scale.
quotes: EOS is designed for owner-operators (what they call Integrators), not for CEOs with a board and shareholders. These two jobs share a superficial resemblance, but in reality? It's apples and oranges.
This transition is such a struggle that 65% of PE firms reported CEO turnover during the holding period, with a good chunk of those being unplanned.
EOS assumes a single decision maker at the top (the Integrator), while the board-accountable CEO faces a more complex reality.
EOS Worldwide itself notes that EOS "was not created for companies with investors and boards of directors.
It is designed from the ground up to put a structure around the CEO who must run a company that has shareholders and a board.
